lead: Memory in an embedded system is not one big pool. It is a set of technologies placed where each fits: ROM (read-only memory) or flash for code that must survive power-off, SRAM (static random-access memory) for fast working data, DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) for large cheap working data, and NAND flash or an SD card for bulk storage. Four questions decide the choice: volatile or not, writable in the field or not, how fast, and how many bits per rupee. The answers show up as fixed addresses in the memory map, and that map is what the processor sees at reset.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.4 for the hardware block diagram and Chapter 1.6 for separate program and data memories.

sections.h3: Volatile memory and the ROM family

blocks.text: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed. SRAM and DRAM are volatile. Non-volatile memory keeps its contents without power. ROM and flash are non-volatile. The ROM family is read-mostly: mask ROM is programmed at the factory with a fixed pattern and is cheapest at high volume. PROM (programmable ROM) is programmed once by the user. EPROM (erasable PROM) is programmed electrically and erased by ultraviolet light through a quartz window; it is slow to erase and now rare. EEPROM (electrically erasable PROM) is erased and written electrically, byte by byte, and has limited endurance. OTP (one-time programmable) behaves like PROM inside a cheap package. Endurance is the number of erase/write cycles a cell or block survives before it may fail. Mask ROM has no field writes, so endurance does not apply. EEPROM may endure about 10⁵ to 10⁶ byte writes. ROM and flash hold the program because it must start after a power cut.

Flash is EEPROM-like but erased in blocks or sectors, not byte by byte. A write is erase-then-program. You cannot overwrite one byte in the middle of a block. NOR flash allows random access and execute-in-place (XiP), so a processor fetches instructions directly from it; it holds code. NAND flash is page-addressed: reads and writes use pages, erases use larger blocks. It is denser and cheaper per bit than NOR, so it holds bulk data. NAND needs bad-block management and a file system or flash translation layer. Endurance is typically 10⁴ to 10⁵ erase cycles per block. That rules out logging every millisecond into on-chip flash: 1000 writes/s would wear a 10⁴-cycle block in about 10 s. Buffer logs in RAM, batch them, or use an SD card.

sections.h3: SRAM, DRAM and the memory map

blocks.text: SRAM stores one bit in a six-transistor cell. It holds data while powered, needs no refresh, and is fast, but it uses many transistors per bit, so density is low and cost per bit high. It is used for registers, on-chip RAM, and caches. DRAM stores one bit as charge on a capacitor with one access transistor. The capacitor leaks, so every row must be refreshed (read and rewritten). DRAM is dense and cheap per bit, slower than SRAM, and used as main memory. SDRAM (synchronous DRAM) is clocked with the bus; DDR (double data rate) SDRAM transfers on both clock edges. A typical microcontroller (MCU) memory map puts flash at address 0 because the reset vector (the first instruction address after reset) lives there. On-chip SRAM sits above it. Peripheral registers (control and data registers for timers, ports, and so on) sit at fixed addresses. The processor fetches code from flash, keeps variables and stack in SRAM, puts large frame buffers in DRAM, and keeps logs and firmware images in NAND or an SD card.

Ask four questions in order. First, must the data survive power-off? If yes, choose ROM, flash, EEPROM, NAND, or an SD card; if no, SRAM or DRAM. Second, must it be written in the field? Mask ROM and OTP cannot; flash and EEPROM can, with block or byte granularity. Third, how fast? Registers and SRAM answer in one cycle; DRAM is slower; NOR flash reads fast but erase and program are slow. Fourth, how many bits per rupee? SRAM is costliest, DRAM cheaper, NAND cheapest per bit. The rule: code in flash, variables and stack in SRAM, large frame buffers in DRAM, logs and firmware images in NAND or an SD card. A small MCU with 64 KB flash and 8 KB SRAM cannot hold an 8-hour millisecond log.

figure.caption: The stack runs from registers at the top to NAND or SD card at the bottom. Flash and ROM sit in the middle: slower than SRAM, but the only level that keeps code without power.

spec.title: The embedded memory hierarchy
spec.aria: A five-level stack from registers at the top down through SRAM, flash, DRAM and NAND flash, marked faster and costlier at the top and slower and cheaper at the bottom.

examples.question: A battery-powered data logger has 12 KB of program code and 1 KB of constant lookup tables. It samples a sensor every 1 ms, 4 bytes per sample, and must keep 8 hours of samples while powered off. Its MCU has 64 KB flash and 8 KB SRAM. (a) How much flash is needed for code and tables? (b) How many bytes are produced in 8 hours? (c) Can the whole log live in on-chip memory? Explain.
steps: Flash for code and tables = 12 KB + 1 KB = 13 KB. The 64 KB flash is enough; 51 KB remains free.
Sample rate = 1 sample per 1 ms = 1000 samples/s.

8 KB SRAM = 8192 bytes; 8192 ÷ 4 = 2048 samples, about 2.048 s at 1 ms. The 64 KB flash holds 65,536 ÷ 4 = 16,384 samples, about 16.4 s, and repeated writes wear the block. The log needs NAND flash or an SD card.
examples.answer: 13 KB flash is enough for code and tables; the logger produces 115,200,000 bytes (115.2 MB, 109.86 MiB) in 8 hours, so the log must go to NAND flash or an SD card, with only a small SRAM buffer on-chip.
examples.check:
code_kb = 12
table_kb = 1
flash_kb = code_kb + table_kb
samples_per_second = 1000
seconds = 8 * 3600
samples = samples_per_second * seconds
total_bytes = samples * 4
mb = total_bytes / 1_000_000
mib = total_bytes / (1024 * 1024)
print(flash_kb)
print(total_bytes)
print(mb)
print(round(mib, 2))

traps: Flash is not byte-writable like EEPROM: erase the whole block, then program it.
SRAM is volatile even though it needs no refresh; DRAM is volatile and needs refresh.
EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light; EEPROM is erased electrically, byte by byte.
NOR and NAND are both flash but not interchangeable: NOR for execute-in-place code, NAND for bulk data with bad-block management.
KB and KiB differ: 115,200,000 bytes is 115.2 MB but 109.86 MiB.

quiz.q: What does volatile mean? Name two volatile memory types.
quiz.a: Contents vanish when power is removed. SRAM and DRAM are volatile.

quiz.q: Which ROM type is erased by ultraviolet light?
Why must flash be erased in blocks before programming? What does that mean for changing one byte?
quiz.a: Erase sets a block to 1s, then program writes 0s. Changing one byte requires copying the block, erasing, and rewriting it.

quiz.q: A NOR flash block has endurance 10⁴ erase cycles. A logger erases one block every 2 s. How long until 10⁴ cycles?
An MCU has 32 KB flash and 4 KB SRAM. Code is 20 KB and constants 2 KB. Free flash? Can a 100 KB log fit on-chip?
quiz.a: Free flash = 32 − (20 + 2) = 10 KB. No, 100 KB log does not fit; use external NAND or SD.

quiz.q: Why do many MCUs put flash at address 0 and the stack in SRAM?
quiz.a: The reset vector is at address 0 and must be non-volatile; flash keeps it without power. The stack changes constantly, so it needs fast writable SRAM, not flash.

quiz.q: Give two reasons NAND flash is a poor choice for execute-in-place code.
quiz.a: NAND is page-addressed, not random-access byte addressable, so fetch is slow and complex. It has bad blocks and needs a translation layer, so direct execution is unreliable.

quiz.q: Why does DRAM need refresh but SRAM not?
quiz.a: DRAM stores charge on a capacitor that leaks. SRAM uses cross-coupled transistors that hold state while powered.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern MCUs often use embedded flash with ECC and store firmware images in external QSPI NOR or eMMC. Wear levelling and flash translation layers spread erase cycles so an SD card survives logs. Universal Flash Storage (UFS) and eMMC are common in phones and automotive clusters. Emerging non-volatile memories such as MRAM and ReRAM aim to combine SRAM speed with flash non-volatility. Search next for wear levelling, flash translation layer, execute-in-place, and memory-mapped I/O.
